claim: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) serve as a surveillance system to repress the expression of nonsense mRNAs that may produce harmful truncated proteins.
source: Here, we report that miRNAs also serve as a surveillance system to repress the expression of nonsense mRNAs that may produce harmful truncated proteins.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental results including deadenylation assays, luciferase assays, and Western blots showing miRNA-mediated repression of nonsense mRNAs.

claim: Upon recognition of the premature termination codon by the translating ribosome, the downstream portion of the coding region of an mRNA is redefined as part of the 3′ untranslated region.
source: Upon recognition of the premature termination codon by the translating ribosome, the downstream portion of the coding region of an mRNA is redefined as part of the 3′ untranslated region
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that miREs downstream of PTCs become functional, as demonstrated in Figure 1A where LastEx-PTC-L7 shows accelerated deadenylation compared to LastEx-L7.

claim: miRNA-responsive elements embedded in the redefined 3′ UTR region can be detected by miRNAs, triggering accelerated mRNA deadenylation and translational inhibition.
source: as a result, the miRNA-responsive elements embedded in this region can be detected by miRNAs, triggering accelerated mRNA deadenylation and translational inhibition.
evidence: Supported by deadenylation assays in Figure 1A showing accelerated poly(A) tail shortening and luciferase assays in Figure 2C-E showing both mRNA reduction and translational repression.

claim: Naturally occurring cancer-causing APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) nonsense mutants which escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) are repressed by miRNA-mediated surveillance.
source: We demonstrate that naturally occurring cancer-causing APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) nonsense mutants which escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) are repressed by miRNA-mediated surveillance.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blots in Figure 3F-G showing changes in truncated APC protein levels upon miR-29a knockdown and overexpression, and RIP assays in Figure 3J-K showing Ago2 association with PTC-APC mRNA.

claim: miRNA-mediated surveillance and exon–exon junction complex-mediated NMD are not mutually exclusive and act additively to enhance the repressive activity.
source: In addition, we show that miRNA-mediated surveillance and exon–exon junction complex-mediated NMD are not mutually exclusive and act additively to enhance the repressive activity.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assays in Figure 4C-D showing that reporters sensitive to both mechanisms (pFL-BRCA1in) exhibit stronger repression than those sensitive to only one mechanism.

claim: Many inherited genetic disorders, such as β-thalassemia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy, are caused by germline nonsense mutations.
source: Indeed, many inherited genetic disorders, such as β-thalassemia (Chang and Kan, 1979) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Koenig et al., 1987; Monaco et al., 1988), are caused by germline nonsense mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on β-thalassemia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

claim: Nonsense mutations in critical tumor suppressor genes are associated with prevalent cancer types such as breast cancer and colorectal cancer.
source: Moreover, nonsense mutations in critical tumor suppressor genes are associated with prevalent cancer types such as breast cancer (Miki et al., 1994) and colorectal cancer (Powell et al., 1992; Rowan et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on breast cancer and colorectal cancer.

claim: Healthy individuals carry dozens of nonsense mutations.
source: A recent large-scale genome-wide study revealed that even healthy individuals carry dozens of nonsense mutations (MacArthur et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a genome-wide study by MacArthur et al., 2012.

claim: Transcriptional errors, mis-splicing, or alternative splicing frequently lead to nonsense mutations.
source: In addition, transcriptional errors, mis-splicing, or even alternative splicing (Danckwardt et al., 2002; Lewis et al., 2003; Wollerton et al., 2004) also frequently lead to nonsense mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on transcriptional errors and splicing.

claim: Cells have evolved a surveillance system known as nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) to eliminate aberrant transcripts.
source: Accordingly, cells have evolved a surveillance system known as nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) to eliminate these aberrant transcripts.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NMD as a quality control mechanism.

claim: An EJC will remain bound to the mRNA and trigger NMD efficiently if the ribosome stalls at a PTC located at least 50 nucleotides upstream of the final exon–exon junction.
source: An EJC will remain bound to the mRNA and trigger NMD efficiently if the ribosome stalls at a PTC located at least 50 nucleotides (nt) upstream of the final exon–exon junction (Maquat, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the '50 nt boundary rule' for EJC-NMD, supported by a citation to Maquat, 2004.

claim: Nonsense transcripts that originate from naturally intronless genes are immune to EJC-NMD.
source: However, nonsense transcripts that originate from naturally intronless genes are immune to EJC-NMD, as are transcripts with PTCs located within the last exon or less than 50 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of EJC-NMD based on the mechanism requiring downstream EJCs.

claim: Transcripts with PTCs located within the last exon or less than 50 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction are immune to EJC-NMD.
source: However, nonsense transcripts that originate from naturally intronless genes are immune to EJC-NMD, as are transcripts with PTCs located within the last exon or less than 50 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the '50 nt boundary rule' for EJC-NMD.

claim: Long 3′ untranslated regions (UTRs) and upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are involved in the degradation of PTC-containing mRNAs.
source: Other EJC-independent NMD mechanisms, such as long 3′ untranslated regions (UTRs) (Buhler et al., 2006; Eberle et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2008; Hogg and Goff, 2010; Zund et al., 2013) and upstream open reading frames (uORFs) (Matsui et al., 2007) are also involved in the degradation of PTC-containing mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature on EJC-independent NMD mechanisms.

claim: miRNAs are processed from hairpin precursors and assemble with Argonaute (Ago) family proteins into RNA-induced silencing complexes (RISCs) to regulate gene expression.
source: In animals, miRNAs are processed from hairpin precursors and assemble with Argonaute (Ago) family proteins into RNA-induced silencing complexes (RISCs) to regulate gene expression (Bartel, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA biogenesis and function, supported by a citation to Bartel, 2004.

claim: miRNAs exert their repressive effects by promoting RNA degradation through accelerated deadenylation and/or by inhibiting translation.
source: By imperfectly base-pairing with miRNA-responsive elements (miREs) in target mRNAs (primarily through nucleotides 2–7, the seed region of the miRNA), miRNAs exert their repressive effects by promoting RNA degradation through accelerated deadenylation and/or by inhibiting translation (Wu and Belasco, 2008b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA mechanisms of action, supported by a citation to Wu and Belasco, 2008b.

claim: miRNAs base-pair with miRNA-responsive elements (miREs) in target mRNAs primarily through nucleotides 2–7, the seed region of the miRNA.
source: By imperfectly base-pairing with miRNA-responsive elements (miREs) in target mRNAs (primarily through nucleotides 2–7, the seed region of the miRNA), miRNAs exert their repressive effects by promoting RNA degradation through accelerated deadenylation and/or by inhibiting translation (Wu and Belasco, 2008b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA-target recognition, supported by a citation to Wu and Belasco, 2008b.

claim: The vast majority of known functional and conserved miREs reside within the 3′ UTR of mRNAs.
source: The vast majority of known functional and conserved miREs reside within the 3′ UTR of mRNAs (Bartel, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRE localization, supported by a citation to Bartel, 2004.

claim: Reports of miRNAs efficiently targeting ORFs are sparse.
source: By contrast, reports of miRNAs efficiently targeting ORFs are sparse (Duursma et al., 2008; Forman et al., 2008; Tay et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2010; Schnall-Levin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to a limited number of studies on ORF targeting by miRNAs.

claim: Recent studies describing the transcriptome-wide identification of miREs revealed prevalent RISC binding in the coding region.
source: Interestingly, recent studies describing the transcriptome-wide identification of miREs revealed prevalent RISC binding in the coding region (Chi et al., 2009; Hafner et al., 2010; Helwak et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to transcriptome-wide CLIP studies.

claim: miRNAs cause expedited removal of the poly(A) tails from their mRNA targets through the recognition of miREs in the 3′ UTR.
source: Previously, we have shown that miRNAs cause expedited removal of the poly(A) tails from their mRNA targets through the recognition of miREs in the 3′ UTR.
evidence: This is supported by a reference to previous work by the authors (Wu et al., 2006) and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: By accelerating the initial and rate-limiting step of mRNA decay, miRNAs efficiently reduce the cellular concentration of their target mRNAs.
source: By accelerating this initial and rate-limiting step of mRNA decay, miRNAs efficiently reduce the cellular concentration of their target mRNAs (Wu et al., 2006; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2006 and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A let-7a miRE inserted in-frame into the ORF of the last exon of β-globin mRNA does not significantly accelerate poly(A) shortening in HeLa-tTA cells where let-7a is naturally abundant.
source: We found that this insertion did not significantly accelerate poly(A) shortening in HeLa-tTA cells, where let-7a is naturally abundant (Figure 1A, compare LastEx-L7 and TBG).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A comparing deadenylation rates of LastEx-L7 and TBG.

claim: ORF miREs are not functionally efficient.
source: This result indicates that ORF miREs are not functionally efficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LastEx-L7 (with an ORF miRE) does not show accelerated deadenylation compared to TBG (Figure 1A).

claim: A point mutation that introduced a PTC 16 nt upstream of the let-7a miRE significantly accelerated the shortening of the 3′ fragment of BG mRNA.
source: Interestingly, a point mutation (AAA to TAA) in the last exon that introduced a PTC 16 nt upstream of the let-7a miRE of LastEx-L7 (LastEx-PTC-L7) significantly accelerated the shortening of the 3′ fragment (Figure 1A, upper portion, compare LastEx-L7 and LastEx-PTC-L7, time points 3 and 4.5), but not the 5′ fragment, of BG mRNA (Figure 1A, bottom portion), a finding indicative of expedited poly(A) removal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A comparing deadenylation rates of LastEx-L7 and LastEx-PTC-L7.

claim: The expedited deadenylation of LastEx-PTC-L7 disappeared when the let-7a miRE was mutated, indicating that the rapid poly(A) removal was specifically induced by endogenous let-7a.
source: The expedited deadenylation disappeared when the let-7a miRE was mutated (LastEx-PTC-L7M), indicating that the rapid poly(A) removal was specifically induced by endogenous let-7a in the cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A comparing LastEx-PTC-L7 and LastEx-PTC-L7M.

claim: The BG mRNA bearing both the let-7a miRE and the upstream PTC decayed much faster than counterparts that lacked the PTC or the let-7a miRE or bore the mutant let-7a miRE, with the half-life decreasing from >6 hr to <3 hr.
source: As a consequence of accelerated deadenylation, the BG mRNA bearing both the let-7a miRE and the upstream PTC decayed much faster than counterparts that lacked the PTC or the let-7a miRE or bore the mutant let-7a miRE, with the half-life decreasing from >6 hr to <3 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mRNA decay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The deadenylation rate of a BG reporter with a PTC located 11 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction was accelerated in a miRNA-dependent manner.
source: Similarly, the deadenylation rate of another BG reporter with a PTC located 11 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction was also accelerated in a miRNA-dependent manner (Figure 1C, compare PTC102-L7 and PTC102-L7M, time points 1.5, 3, and 4.5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing PTC102-L7 and PTC102-L7M.

claim: Expedited poly(A) shortening was not observed for BG mRNA bearing the PTC in the last exon or 11 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction but no downstream miRE.
source: Expedited poly(A) shortening was not observed for BG mRNA bearing the PTC in the last exon or 11 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction but no downstream miRE (Figure 1A, LastEx-PTC and Figure 1C, PTC102), because the PTC alone is unable to trigger EJC-NMD when located in the last exon or less than 50 nt upstream of the last exon–exon junction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A (LastEx-PTC) and Figure 1C (PTC102), and explained by the known limitations of EJC-NMD.

claim: miRNA-mediated deadenylation of nonsense mRNAs is not miRNA-type-specific.
source: Similar results were obtained with BG reporters containing one miR-21 miRE (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C and data not shown), providing evidence that miRNA-mediated deadenylation of nonsense mRNAs is not miRNA-type-specific.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with miR-21 miREs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: A BG reporter with a retained last intron that creates a PTC 505 nt upstream of the let-7a miRE underwent rapid deadenylation in a miRNA-dependent manner.
source: As expected, we found that TBG-IR-L7 underwent rapid deadenylation in a miRNA-dependent manner; and that absence of the downstream miRE (TBG-IR) or mutations in the miRE seed region (TBG-IR-L7M) completely abolished this accelerated deadenylation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1D comparing TBG-IR-L7, TBG-IR, and TBG-IR-L7M.

claim: Blocking translation by placing a large stem-loop structure at the 5′ UTR caused LastEx-L7 mRNA to undergo rapid miRNA-mediated deadenylation and decay.
source: As expected, blocking translation in this manner caused LastEx-L7 mRNA, which normally is deadenylated and decays slowly, to undergo rapid miRNA-mediated deadenylation and decay (half-life of >6 hr vs <3 hr) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B comparing hp-LastEx-L7 and hp-LastEx-L7M.

claim: Translating ribosomes interfere with miRNA-RISC binding to the miREs located in the ORF and thus mask their repressive function.
source: suggesting that translating ribosomes may indeed have interfered with miRNA-RISC binding to the miREs located in the ORF and thus masked their repressive function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking translation unmasks ORF miREs (Figure 1E), consistent with a previous study by Gu et al., 2009.

claim: miRNAs selectively accelerate the deadenylation of nonsense mRNAs by stably binding to miREs in the ORF downstream of the PTC.
source: Together, these data suggest that miRNAs selectively accelerate the deadenylation of nonsense mRNAs by stably binding to miREs in the ORF downstream of the PTC.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experimental results showing PTC-dependent acceleration of deadenylation (Figures 1A, 1C, 1D, 1E).

claim: The immunity of PTC-free mRNA to miRNA-mediated repression may be due to masking of ORF miREs by the translating ribosomes.
source: The immunity of PTC-free mRNA to miRNA-mediated repression may be due to masking of ORF miREs by the translating ribosomes, which is consistent with a previous study using constitutively transcribed luciferase reporters (Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by a citation to Gu et al., 2009.

claim: Measurement of the steady-state mRNA level showed specific and significant repression of TAA-2E in the presence of miR-125b.
source: Measurement of the steady-state mRNA level by qRT-PCR showed specific and significant repression of TAA-2E in the presence of miR-125b (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Measurement of luciferase activity revealed an even greater reduction of the PTC-containing reporter at the protein level than at the mRNA level.
source: Moreover, the measurement of luciferase activity revealed an even greater reduction of the PTC-containing reporter at the protein level (Figure 2D), indicating that translational repression plays a prominent role in the repression of nonsense messages by miRNAs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase activity data shown in Figure 2D and the calculated repression ratios in Figure 2E.

claim: Translational repression plays a prominent role in the repression of nonsense messages by miRNAs.
source: Moreover, the measurement of luciferase activity revealed an even greater reduction of the PTC-containing reporter at the protein level (Figure 2D), indicating that translational repression plays a prominent role in the repression of nonsense messages by miRNAs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of protein and mRNA repression ratios shown in Figure 2E.

claim: An miRE has to be located at least 10 nt downstream of the PTC to trigger miRNA-mediated repression effectively.
source: Measurement of luciferase activity revealed that an miRE has to be located at least 10 nt downstream of the PTC to trigger miRNA-mediated repression effectively (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase activity data shown in Figure 2G testing different miRE positions relative to the PTC.

claim: The size of the footprint of RISC is much smaller than that of the EJC.
source: This observation defines a distinct boundary rule for miRNAs to successfully repress PTC-containing messages and also suggests that the size of the footprint of RISC is much smaller than that of the EJC, which makes miRNA-mediated surveillance more versatile in recognizing and repressing nonsense mRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the 10 nt boundary rule for miRNA-mediated surveillance compared to the 50 nt boundary rule for EJC-NMD.

claim: miRNA-mediated surveillance is more versatile than EJC-NMD in recognizing and repressing nonsense mRNAs.
source: This observation defines a distinct boundary rule for miRNAs to successfully repress PTC-containing messages and also suggests that the size of the footprint of RISC is much smaller than that of the EJC, which makes miRNA-mediated surveillance more versatile in recognizing and repressing nonsense mRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the smaller boundary requirement (10 nt vs 50 nt) for miRNA-mediated surveillance compared to EJC-NMD.

claim: A PTC can potentiate miRNA-mediated deadenylation and translational inhibition of nonsense mRNAs, via redefinition of ORF/3′ UTR identities and unmasking of downstream miREs.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that a PTC can potentiate miRNA-mediated deadenylation and translational inhibition of nonsense mRNAs, via redefinition of ORF/3′ UTR identities and unmasking of downstream miREs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Most of the mutations in the APC gene that have been identified in clinical studies are point mutations or frameshift indels that create a PTC and result in the expression of a truncated version of the APC protein.
source: Most of the mutations in the APC gene that have been identified in clinical studies are point mutations or frameshift indels that create a PTC and result in the expression of a truncated version of the APC protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APC mutations in colorectal cancer.

claim: The majority of known APC mutations are clustered in a hotspot region (designated as the MCR) within the last exon of the ORF.
source: Interestingly, the majority of known APC mutations are clustered in a hotspot region (designated as the MCR in Figure 3A) within the last exon of the ORF (Miyoshi et al., 1992)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miyoshi et al., 1992 and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: APC mutations in the MCR render these mutants immune to EJC-NMD.
source: Interestingly, the majority of known APC mutations are clustered in a hotspot region (designated as the MCR in Figure 3A) within the last exon of the ORF (Miyoshi et al., 1992), rendering these mutants immune to EJC-NMD.
evidence: This is inferred from the location of the MCR in the last exon, which is beyond the reach of EJC-NMD based on the 50 nt boundary rule.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis predicts numerous potential miREs between the MCR and the native stop codon in APC mRNA.
source: Meanwhile, bioinformatic analysis based on the seed match rule predicts numerous potential miREs between the MCR and the native stop codon in APC mRNA.
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using the seed match rule.

claim: Multiple miREs in the PTC-STOP region of APC mRNA exhibited specific responses to cognate miRNAs.
source: Multiple miREs exhibited specific responses to the cognate miRNAs (Figure 3B), which verifies their functionality.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Western blotting revealed a marked increase in protein expression for the minigene constructs with mutant miREs compared to wild-type miREs.
source: Western blotting revealed a marked increase in protein expression for the minigene constructs with mutant miREs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the context of the natural APC 3′ UTR, the PTC was able to potentiate repression by miR-29a miREs originally located in the ORF.
source: Western blotting showed that, in the context of the natural APC 3′ UTR, the PTC was still able to potentiate repression by miR-29a miREs originally located in the ORF (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: ORF miREs unmasked by an upstream PTC are fully functional in the presence of repression by 3′ UTR miREs.
source: These observations indicate that ORF miREs unmasked by an upstream PTC are fully functional in the presence of repression by 3′ UTR miREs.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects observed in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 when both ORF and 3′ UTR miREs are present.

claim: SW480 is a colorectal cell line that naturally expresses a truncated APC protein caused by a PTC mutation at codon 1338.
source: SW480 is a colorectal cell line that naturally expresses a truncated APC protein (caused by a PTC mutation at codon 1338) that can be readily detected by Western blotting with a specific antibody (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: An approximate twofold increase in truncated APC expression was observed for SW480 cells in which miR-29a was knocked down.
source: An approximate twofold increase in truncated APC expression was observed for SW480 cells in which miR-29a was knocked down (Figure 3F, upper panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The knockdown of miR-29a caused a ∼1.6-fold increase of PTC-APC mRNA.
source: We also measured the mRNA level of PTC-APC in SW480 cells and found that the knockdown of miR-29a caused a ∼1.6-fold increase of PTC-APC mRNA (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The abundance of miR-26a remained unchanged upon miR-29a knockdown in SW480 cells.
source: by contrast, the abundance of an untargeted endogenous miRNA, miR-26a, remained unchanged (Figure 3F, bottom panel), suggesting the upregulation observed for PTC-APC was specifically induced by the inhibition of miR-29a.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Northern blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The upregulation of PTC-APC was specifically induced by the inhibition of miR-29a.
source: by contrast, the abundance of an untargeted endogenous miRNA, miR-26a, remained unchanged (Figure 3F, bottom panel), suggesting the upregulation observed for PTC-APC was specifically induced by the inhibition of miR-29a.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific knockdown of miR-29a without affecting miR-26a, and the corresponding increase in PTC-APC.

claim: The amount of WT-APC protein remained unchanged after the induction of miR-29a expression to much higher levels in HEK293 cells.
source: The amount of WT-APC protein remained unchanged after the induction of miR-29a expression to much higher levels in the cells (Figure 3H) because the miR-29a miREs are located within the PTC-STOP region but not the 3′ UTR of APC mRNA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: SW480 cells that overexpress miR-29a produced a lower amount of truncated APC compared to cells that overexpressed a non-functional small RNA.
source: In contrast, SW480 cells that overexpress miR-29a produced a lower amount of truncated APC compared to cells that overexpressed a non-functional small RNA that did not affect the already high expression levels of endogenous miR-29a (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: miR-29a specifically represses the PTC-APC and does not impair the expression of WT-APC.
source: These results support that miR-29a specifically represses the PTC-APC and does not impair the expression of WT-APC.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of miR-29a on PTC-APC (repressed) versus WT-APC (unchanged) shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: The level of endogenous PTC-APC mRNA associated with Ago2 showed a mild but reproducible decrease when miR-29a was knocked down.
source: The level of endogenous PTC-APC mRNA associated with Ago2 showed a mild but reproducible decrease when miR-29a was knocked down (Figure 3J)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RIP assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The level of endogenous PTC-APC mRNA associated with Ago2 showed a significant increase upon miR-29a overexpression in SW480 cells.
source: The level of endogenous PTC-APC mRNA associated with Ago2 showed a mild but reproducible decrease when miR-29a was knocked down (Figure 3J) and a significant increase upon miR-29a overexpression in SW480 cells (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RIP assay data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The 3′ UTR of APC mRNA contains no miR-29a miREs.
source: The 3′ UTR of APC mRNA contains no miR-29a miREs, which was determined by comparing the expression of a luciferase reporter bearing a full-length APC 3′ UTR in the presence of miR-29a versus a negative control small RNA (siNC) (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: In the presence of miR-29a, the APC-PTC1450 mRNA that harbors wild-type miR-29a miREs has a much stronger association with Ago2 than does its counterpart that contains the mutant miREs.
source: In the presence of miR-29a, the APC-PTC1450 mRNA that harbors wild-type miR-29a miREs has a much stronger association with Ago2 than does its counterpart that contains the mutant miREs (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RIP assay data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: A mutant version of the miR-29a mimic that restored base-pairing of the 2–7 seed with the mutant miR-29a miRE also restored repression of APC mRNA.
source: In addition, a mutant version of the miR-29a mimic that restored base-pairing of the 2–7 seed with the mutant miR-29a miRE also restored repression of APC mRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Repression of PTC-APC expression is achieved through the direct interaction of miR-29a with the miREs mapped in the study.
source: In addition, a mutant version of the miR-29a mimic that restored base-pairing of the 2–7 seed with the mutant miR-29a miRE also restored repression of APC mRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), supporting the conclusion that repression of PTC-APC expression is achieved through the direct interaction of miR-29a with the miREs we mapped.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and the RIP assays in Figures 3J-M.

claim: The expression of a naturally occurring nonsense mRNA is selectively repressed by endogenous miRNAs in the cells.
source: Altogether, these observations represent novel evidence that the expression of a naturally occurring nonsense mRNA is selectively repressed by endogenous miRNAs in the cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the APC experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most BRCA1 nonsense mutants contain introns downstream of the PTC and are EJC-NMD-sensitive.
source: Unlike APC, mutations that lead to the expression of a truncated version of BRCA1 are scattered along the ORF (Castilla et al., 1994); therefore, most BRCA1 nonsense mutants contain introns downstream of the PTC and are EJC-NMD-sensitive (Perrin-Vidoz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on BRCA1 mutations.

claim: The expression level of pFL-BRCA1in was significantly lower compared to pFL-BRCA1, indicating that EJC-NMD was contributing to the repressive activity.
source: The expression level of pFL-BRCA1in was significantly lower compared to pFL-BRCA1, indicating that EJC-NMD was contributing to the repressive activity (Figure 4C, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Knockdown of GW182 caused a significant increase in the expression level of pFL-BRCA1, indicating that miRNAs were involved in the repression.
source: When GW182, a key component of RISC, was knocked down >70% by small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) in HeLa-tTA cells (Figure 4C, right panel), the expression level of pFL-BRCA1 was significantly increased, which indicates that miRNAs were indeed involved in the repression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay and Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Knockdown of GW182 caused a comparable extent of upregulation of pFL-BRCA1in, suggesting that miRNA-mediated repression of PTC-containing mRNAs is independent of the presence of downstream introns.
source: More importantly, knockdown of GW182 also caused a comparable extent of upregulation of pFL-BRCA1in, suggesting that miRNA-mediated repression of PTC-containing mRNAs is independent of the presence of downstream introns (Figure 4C, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C and inferred from the similar effects on both reporters.

claim: miRNA-mediated surveillance and EJC-NMD are not mutually exclusive.
source: Thus, miRNA-mediated surveillance and EJC-NMD are not mutually exclusive, and the repressive effects caused by both mechanisms are additive.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both mechanisms can act on the same transcript (pFL-BRCA1in) as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The repressive effects caused by miRNA-mediated surveillance and EJC-NMD are additive.
source: Thus, miRNA-mediated surveillance and EJC-NMD are not mutually exclusive, and the repressive effects caused by both mechanisms are additive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data in Figure 4D showing that pFL-BRCA1in (sensitive to both mechanisms) exhibits stronger repression than reporters sensitive to only one mechanism.

claim: A markedly stronger repression was observed for the reporter expected to be sensitive to both EJC-NMD and miRNA (pFL-BRCA1in) when co-transfected with miR-137 or miR-544.
source: Importantly, a markedly stronger repression was observed for the reporter expected to be sensitive to both EJC-NMD and miRNA (pFL-BRCA1in) when co-transfected with miR-137 or miR-544 but not when co-transfected with a control small RNA (Figure 4D, compare black and white bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 11 of the 16 candidates from HCT-116 cells contained at least one functional miRE in the PTC-STOP regions.
source: We found that 11 of the 16 candidates contained at least one functional miRE in the PTC-STOP regions (Figure 4E–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 4E-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several candidates, such as ITGA6, USP1, and PPM1J, harbored multiple functional miREs that were responsive to different miRNAs.
source: Several of these candidates, such as ITGA6, USP1, and PPM1J, harbored multiple functional miREs that were responsive to different miRNAs (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 4F-H.

claim: Other candidates, such as KTN1 and RAD54L2, contained at least one strong miRE.
source: Other candidates, such as KTN1 and RAD54L2, contained at least one strong miRE (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: miRNA-mediated surveillance may serve as a general mechanism that downregulates various nonsense mRNAs in human cells.
source: Together, our results strongly support the view that miRNA-mediated surveillance may serve as a general mechanism that downregulates various nonsense mRNAs in human cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the validation of multiple candidates from HCT-116 cells shown in Figures 4E-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: miRNA-mediated surveillance is EJC-independent.
source: Unlike classic NMD, miRNA-mediated surveillance is EJC-independent and recognizes its targets only if an miRE is embedded in the PTC-STOP region (Figure 1A) at a position as close as 10 nt downstream of the PTC (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing that miRNA-mediated surveillance works on transcripts without downstream introns (Figure 1A) and has a different boundary rule (10 nt) than EJC-NMD (50 nt).

claim: miRNA-mediated surveillance recognizes its targets only if an miRE is embedded in the PTC-STOP region at a position as close as 10 nt downstream of the PTC.
source: Unlike classic NMD, miRNA-mediated surveillance is EJC-independent and recognizes its targets only if an miRE is embedded in the PTC-STOP region (Figure 1A) at a position as close as 10 nt downstream of the PTC (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1A and 2F,G.

claim: The repressive influence of miRNA is enhanced by combining accelerated mRNA degradation and translational inhibition.
source: The repressive influence of miRNA is enhanced by combining accelerated mRNA degradation and translational inhibition (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figures 2C-E showing both mRNA reduction and greater protein reduction.

claim: miRNA-mediated surveillance can work together with other surveillance mechanisms, such as EJC-NMD, in an additive manner.
source: Furthermore, miRNA-mediated surveillance can work together with other surveillance mechanisms, such as EJC-NMD, in an additive manner (Figure 4C,D), which strengthens the repressive activity and expands the substrate spectrum of the cellular mRNA quality control system.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figures 4C,D showing additive effects.

claim: An estimated one-third of genetic diseases are associated with truncated proteins produced from nonsense mRNAs.
source: An estimated one-third of genetic diseases are associated with truncated proteins produced from nonsense mRNAs (Kuzmiak and Maquat, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuzmiak and Maquat, 2006.

claim: Truncated BRCA1 has been shown to antagonize wild-type BRCA1 function in a dominant-negative manner.
source: Indeed, truncated BRCA1 has been shown to antagonize wild-type BRCA1 function in a dominant-negative manner (Fan et al., 2001; Sylvain et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fan et al., 2001 and Sylvain et al., 2002.

claim: Several lines of evidence support the view that truncated APC contributes to colorectal cancer by causing spindle misalignment that eventually leads to chromosomal instability.
source: and several lines of evidence support the view that truncated APC contributes to colorectal cancer by causing spindle misalignment that eventually leads to chromosomal instability (Fodde et al., 2001; Tighe et al., 2004; Quyn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fodde et al., 2001, Tighe et al., 2004, and Quyn et al., 2010.

claim: Many unconventional miREs exist in animals.
source: Recent studies have revealed that many unconventional miREs exist in animals (Shin et al., 2010; Helwak et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shin et al., 2010 and Helwak et al., 2013.

claim: A luciferase reporter harboring the miR-29a miREs from the PTC-STOP region of APC nonsense mutant is efficiently repressed only in colon-derived SW480 cells but not in kidney-derived HEK293 cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that a luciferase reporter harboring the miR-29a miREs from the PTC-STOP region of APC nonsense mutant is efficiently repressed only in colon-derived SW480 cells but is not in kidney-derived HEK293 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B,D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B,D.

claim: The tissue-specific repression of APC nonsense mutant correlates with the relatively high abundance of miR-29a in SW480 cells and its undetectable level of expression in HEK293 cells.
source: which correlates well with the relatively high abundance of miR-29a in SW480 cells and its undetectable level of expression in HEK293 cells (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between miR-29a expression levels and repression efficiency shown in Figures 3F-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B,D.

claim: A nonsense mRNA may have a very different fate in distinct tissues depending on which miRNAs are highly expressed.
source: This finding implies that a nonsense mRNA may have a very different fate in distinct tissues depending on which miRNAs are highly expressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific repression observed for APC nonsense mutant.

claim: The expression of many miRNAs are tissue- or cell type-specific and are dynamically regulated during cell differentiation or under different physiological conditions.
source: It is well established that the expression of many miRNAs are tissue- or cell type-specific and are dynamically regulated during cell differentiation or under different physiological conditions (Houbaviy et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2005; Marsit et al., 2006; Landgraf et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some nonsense mRNAs may escape miRNA-mediated surveillance due to the lack of expression of certain miRNAs in some tissues or under some stress conditions, thereby increasing the risk of tissue-specific diseases.
source: Some nonsense mRNAs may escape miRNA-mediated surveillance due to the lack of expression of certain miRNAs in some tissues or under some stress conditions, thereby increasing the risk of tissue-specific diseases.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the tissue-specific expression of miRNAs and the observed tissue-specific repression.

claim: Approximately 35% of alternatively spliced gene products contain PTCs.
source: In addition to many identified nonsense messages resulting from genomic mutations, evidence suggests that ∼35% of alternatively spliced gene products contain PTCs (Lewis et al., 2003; Wollerton et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2003 and Wollerton et al., 2004.

claim: Transcripts with retained introns are efficiently degraded by miRNAs.
source: Transcripts with retained introns, for example, are efficiently degraded by miRNAs, as shown by our BG reporter assays (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: More than 10% of Ago-CLIP reads map to introns.
source: Consistent with this idea, more than 10% of Ago-CLIP reads map to introns (Chi et al., 2009; Hafner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published Ago-CLIP studies.

claim: Hundreds of PTC-containing transcripts generated by intron retention are bound by Ago in the PTC-STOP regions.
source: Our computational analyses of transcriptome and published Ago-CLIP sequencing data from two human cell lines revealed that hundreds of PTC-containing transcripts generated by intron retention are indeed bound by Ago in the PTC-STOP regions (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of published data.

claim: miRNAs have a new role in mRNA quality control.
source: Taken together, we have uncovered a new role for miRNAs in mRNA quality control.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: The miRNA-mediated surveillance system acts in parallel with other systems, such as EJC-NMD, to provide extra protection for the cells against nonsense mutations.
source: This miRNA-mediated surveillance system acts in parallel with other systems, such as EJC-NMD, to provide extra protection for the cells against nonsense mutations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the additive effects observed in Figure 4C,D.

claim: APC and BRCA1 nonsense mutant mRNAs are downregulated by multiple miRNAs that specifically target the PTC-STOP regions.
source: We have also demonstrated that APC and BRCA1 nonsense mutant mRNAs are downregulated by multiple miRNAs that specifically target the PTC-STOP regions, thereby providing a feasible means to eliminate such deleterious nonsense transcripts without impairing their wild-type counterparts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results for APC (Figure 3) and BRCA1 (Figure 4).

claim: miRNA-mediated surveillance provides a feasible means to eliminate deleterious nonsense transcripts without impairing their wild-type counterparts.
source: We have also demonstrated that APC and BRCA1 nonsense mutant mRNAs are downregulated by multiple miRNAs that specifically target the PTC-STOP regions, thereby providing a feasible means to eliminate such deleterious nonsense transcripts without impairing their wild-type counterparts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WT-APC is not affected by miR-29a (Figure 3H) while PTC-APC is repressed (Figure 3G).
